title: Salt the endpoint key
prompt: One endpoint takes most of the traffic, so split it with a salt from 0 to 3 taken from the request id. Write `solve(api_requests)` so it returns how many requests fall in each `(endpoint, salt)` group, as `endpoint`, `salt` and `requests`.
rules: `salt` is the remainder of `F.hash("request_id")` by 4, always from 0 to 3, never negative. A missing request id still gets a salt.
One row per `endpoint` and `salt` that has requests. Requests with no endpoint form groups of their own.
`requests` counts every request in the group. Return only these three columns, in this order.
hints: `F.hash(...)` can be negative. Which function from the lesson gives a remainder that never is?
`F.pmod(F.hash("request_id"), F.lit(4))` is the salt; add it with `select(..., ....alias("salt"))`.
Group by both columns and count rows with `F.count("*")`, which counts a row even when its request id is missing.
explanation: The salt is `F.pmod(F.hash("request_id"), F.lit(4))`: the hash is a whole number that can be negative, and `pmod` takes a remainder that's always 0 to 3. The `%` operator keeps the sign, so it would make salts like -2 that don't match the salts on the other side of a salted join. Then `groupBy("endpoint", "salt").agg(F.count("*").alias("requests"))`. The hot endpoint now spreads over up to four groups, while the salt depends only on the request id, so the same request always gets the same salt. Hashing the endpoint instead would give every row of a key the same salt and split nothing.
